items.title: Beyond XAI: a claim-specific translation matrix for cancer biomarkers and therapeutic targets
items.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly used in molecular and multimodal oncology to identify features that influence machine-learning predictions. A model-important feature may subsequently be described as a biomarker, mechanistic driver or therapeutic target, although these labels represent distinct scientific claims requiring different evidence. We propose the XAI Biomarker Translation Matrix, a claim-specific conceptual framework separating explanation evidence (E), biological evidence (B) and translational evidence (T). A claim gate routes XAI-prioritised candidates into three validation pathways: diagnostic, prognostic or treatment-predictive biomarkers; mechanistic therapeutic targets; and tumour-selective delivery targets. The explanation dimension is XAI-specific and addresses whether attribution is defined, stable, faithful and reproducible, whereas the biological and translational dimensions connect the attributed feature to claim-appropriate evidence. Claim-evidence concordance requires terminology to remain no stronger than the evidence demonstrated for the intended use, and falsification-first translation asks investigators to prespecify the observation most capable of challenging the proposed interpretation. Complementing established AI-reporting, biomarker-validation and target-assessment standards, the matrix adds an XAI-specific explanation-evidence layer and an explicit claim gate linking attribution to claim-specific evidence and terminology: XAI prioritises candidates; the claim determines the validation pathway.

items.title: Bias in AI video interview evaluations: Effects of autistic-associated behaviors and debiasing procedures
items.abstract: Adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) face employment disparities despite possessing strengths valued in the workplace. One barrier is the interview, where impressions often form from nonverbal cues that commonly differ in ASD and contribute to negative evaluations. Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in hiring, whether these behaviors elicit AI bias is unclear. This study examined whether large language models (LLMs) assign lower ratings to candidates displaying autistic-associated behaviors and whether a debiasing procedure reduces these effects. Three LLMs rated a candidate in mock interview clips across four conditions: control (neurotypical behavior), limited eye contact, monotone speech, and low conversational reciprocity. The LLMs rated interpersonal and cognitive attributes and overall hireability before and after exposure to pro-neurodiversity research. Ratings were lower in all non-control conditions and increased after debiasing. These findings suggest LLMs may replicate bias toward neurodivergent applicants, but this bias can be mitigated.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Book of Abstracts - 13th GEIA Seminar
items.abstract: The thirteenth edition of the GEIA Seminar brings together 48 speakers from 31 institutions across 15 countries, spanning Europe, Asia, Oceania, North and South America. The presenters and participants come from universities, research institutes, airlines, civil aviation authorities, air traffic control organizations, and private language institutions. This geographical and intellectual diversity is one of the seminar’s greatest assets. It allows us to examine familiar challenges through different lenses, learn from different operational and educational contexts, and strengthen the international connections that are essential to the development of our field. The program reflects the breadth and dynamism of current research in Aeronautical English and related areas. Our discussions range from language as a human factor in aviation safety, pilot–controller communication, shared situational awareness, and communication breakdowns to language policy, language description, and the complexities of accent comprehensibility in international aviation. The presentations also explore language assessment and proficiency testing, including questions of validity, communicative efficiency, and the competencies required of Aviation English trainers and assessors.

items.title: BRD-Stereo: Bilateral Reliability Distillation for Lightweight Zero-Shot Stereo Matching
items.abstract: Stereo foundation models provide strong cross-domain generalization but remain computationally expensive for real-time and resource-constrained deployment. We propose BRD-Stereo, a bilateral reliability distillation framework that transfers foundation-model stereo knowledge to a lightweight BANet-style student. BRD-Stereo treats reciprocal left–right correspondence after geometric warping as an exchange symmetry and uses localized symmetry violations from occlusion or mismatching to reduce teacher reliability. BRD-Stereo models the spatial reliability of teacher supervision and aligns different forms of teacher knowledge with the student’s detail/smooth aggregation structure. The detail branch receives boundary- and gradient-aware supervision, while the smooth branch is guided by low-frequency disparity consistency and local plane regularization. Reliability cues from left–right consistency, image disparity edge agreement, local regularity, occlusion-aware validity, and available teacher confidence weight the pseudo-label objectives. Sliced score distribution distillation transfers a locally softened disparity target around the teacher prediction without requiring full teacher cost volume supervision. Experiments on Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury show consistent gains over plain pseudo-label distillation, with the largest improvements concentrated in boundary, occlusion, weak-texture, and large-disparity regions while preserving BANet-scale inference efficiency.

items.title: Bridging Clinical Prediction and Workplace Exposure: A Data-Driven Risk Stratification and Prediction Model for Occupational Respiratory Diseases.
items.abstract: Abstract Occupational respiratory disease (ORD) surveillance remains largely reactive, with diagnosis often occurring only after clinically significant symptoms develop. Existing risk stratification tools are primarily clinically derived and rarely incorporate occupational exposure variables such as exposure intensity, duration, and workplace hazards, limiting early identification of at-risk workers. This review synthesizes current evidence on predictive modelling and risk stratification tools for respiratory diseases, evaluates their applicability to occupational health, and proposes a data-driven framework for proactive risk stratification. A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2021 and 2025. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms related to occupational respiratory diseases, predictive modelling, prognostic tools, and occupational exposure assessment were combined using Boolean operators. Extracted data included study characteristics, modelling approaches, predictors, and model performance metrics, which were narratively synthesized using thematic mapping. Of 618 records identified, six representative evidence approaches were retained for detailed comparative synthesis. Clinical models such as BODE and DOSE provided useful prognostic information but lacked occupational exposure parameters. Exposure-based approaches showed associations between cumulative exposure and respiratory outcomes, while a meta-analysis of machine-learning models for acute respiratory distress syndrome reported a pooled AUC of 0.7407. Key predictors included age, smoking status, lung function, and exposure-related factors. Current reactive and clinically focused approaches limit effective ORD prevention. Integrating occupational exposure variables into predictive, data-driven risk stratification frameworks is essential for early identification of high-risk workers. The proposed ORDiRS framework represents a step toward proactive occupational health surveillance in industrial settings.

items.title: Cancer Detection Using AI-based Techniques
items.abstract: In the medical field, artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have driven significant advancements, particularly in cancer detection and treatment. AI’s ability to mimic human cognition, such as intelligent behavior and critical reasoning, is invaluable for analyzing complex medical data. AI has the potential to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, and patient outcomes of cancer detection, given the disease’s pervasive global impact. AI in imaging diagnostics reduces radiologists’ workload and increases cancer screening sensitivity, contributing to decreased incidence of this deadly disease. This chapter outlines biomedical image processing fundamentals, including pre-processing, feature extraction, and segmentation. It then explores various AI-based techniques in cancer diagnosis, such as image analysis, CAD, pathology analysis, genetic analysis, and risk assessment. This chapter discusses AI algorithms like convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, recurrent neural networks, GANs, support vector machines, and neural networks in cancer detection. Real-world case studies demonstrate AI’s effective use in breast cancer detection via 60 mammography, CT-based lung cancer screening, pathology-based diagnosis, and genomics-based personalized treatment. This chapter addresses challenges and future directions, including ethical and regulatory concerns and AI integration with metaverse and exascale computation to enhance cancer detection.

items.title: Capacidad institucional para la adopción responsable de inteligencia artificial en el sector público ecuatoriano: Desafíos y oportunidades para la gestión pública
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector presents opportunities to transform administrative processes and services, but it demands institutional capacities that ensure responsible, transparent, and sustainable use. This study aimed to analyze the institutional readiness of the Ecuadorian public sector for the responsible adoption of AI. A qualitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and exploratory-descriptive study was conducted. Twenty key informants from various Ecuadorian public institutions were selected using purposive sampling. The results revealed uneven and evolving institutional readiness. While institutions possess basic digital infrastructure, receptive staff, and initial experience with AI tools, they exhibit limitations in interoperability, specialized training, planning, and systematization of AI adoption. The main gaps were concentrated in governance, the absence of specific protocols, data protection, transparency, human oversight, and the definition of responsibilities. The study concludes that the responsible adoption of AI requires the joint strengthening of technological, human, organizational, and regulatory capacities. The main challenge lies in bridging the gap between emerging technologies and the institutional maturity needed to integrate AI securely, traceably, and in a way that strengthens Ecuadorian public administration.

items.title: CarD-T: LLM Automated Literature Review for the Nomination & Analysis of Potential Human Carcinogens
items.abstract: CarD-T is an automated pipeline that combines transformer-based machine learning with probabilistic analysis to identify potential carcinogens from biomedical literature. The framework processes accumulating scientific publications, applies a trained Named Entity Recognition (NER) model to extract potential carcinogenic entities, and Probabilistic Carcinogen Denomination (or PCarD) to analyze temporal trends in evidence shifts. This approach enables classification of candidates through Bayesian temporal analysis, overcoming limitations of traditional manual literature review methods.

items.title: CAREERPILOT AI
items.abstract: The increasing competition in the employment market has created significant challenges for students and job seekers in preparing effective resumes, identifying relevant skills, and performing effectively in interviews. Existing career-support systems commonly address individual tasks such as resume screening, job recommendation, or interview preparation, while providing limited integration and personalization. This paper proposes CareerPilot AI, an intelligent career assistance system that integrates resume analysis, Applicant Tracking System evaluation, job-description matching, skill-gap identification, AI-based mock interviews, response evaluation, and personalized learning-roadmap generation. The proposed system uses Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, semantic matching, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation to process user information and generate context-aware recommendations. A web-based architecture using Streamlit and FastAPI or Flask is proposed, with PDF parsing libraries for resume extraction and vector databases for retrieval-based services. The evaluation framework measures resume parsing accuracy, resume-job matching performance, skill-gap identification, interview-response evaluation, response time, and usability. The system is designed to provide an integrated digital career mentor that connects a candidate's current profile with target job requirements and subsequent preparation activities. Actual experimental results will be obtained after implementation and testing.

items.title: Changing preference of university students in subject selection at undergraduate level: A qualitative study in Peshawar, Pakistan
items.abstract: Subject choice of undergraduate students has shifted from the traditional ones to the market-oriented ones such as computer and allied health sciences. This trend is more felt in the recent years in many public sectors universities in Pakistan which are forced to close certain disciplines while opening market oriented courses and degrees to attract students. This study aimed to find out the factors responsible for this trend. A qualitative research design was used in which data was collected from 20 participants (10 students and 10 faculty members) purposively selected from different disciplines at University of Peshawar, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Thematic analysis was used as data analysis techniques, leading to the emergence of five themes: intrinsic motivation and aptitude; evolving subjects and marketability; social desirability, influence of family, peer, social media, and subject prestige; the purported neoliberalism; and the increasing marketability and importance of disciplines such as computer sciences and allied health sciences. These results show that students' choices of subjects are the result of various determinants including personal, social, economic, structural and technological. Students are more likely to study technology and health-related areas due to the improved marketability and employment opportunities, while the traditional disciplines of social sciences and humanities are seen as limiting their chances of employment and reducing their social standing.

items.title: ChatGPT and mathematical modeling of motion for teaching linear functions in secondary education
items.abstract: This exploratory study analyzes the pedagogical mediation conditions under which ChatGPT's intervention in mathematical modeling amplifies coordination among semiotic registers and favors functional thinking. Twelve second-year secondary school students participated in four teams that modeled the rectilinear motion of a person captured on video and constructed piecewise linear functions. From the articulation between the theory of semiotic representations and Realistic Mathematics Education, the study documented how the teams coordinated the four registers when interacting with ChatGPT. The analysis identifies four conditions that made that mediation productive: the selection of a contextualized situation, the iterative refinement of the prompt, the open stance of the teacher, and the availability of multiple representations as an object of contrast. Given its limited scope, the results offer a first approach to how generative artificial intelligence redistributes cognitive work toward conceptual analysis, and require replication in other groups.

items.title: ChatGPT in Teacher Education: Reducing Pre-Service Teachers’ Cognitive Load
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, its implications for teacher candidates’ cognitive processes warrant closer attention. This mixed-methods study examined the use of ChatGPT during lesson planning in the teaching practicum, focusing on perceived cognitive load, patterns of material use, and teacher candidates’ experiences. Twenty-four fourth-year teacher candidates participated in a six-week implementation in which they used ChatGPT to prepare lesson plans and instructional activities. Quantitative data were collected using a cognitive load rating scale, and qualitative data were obtained from weekly reflective narratives. Perceived cognitive load decreased significantly following the six-week implementation. Participants were also more likely to use ChatGPT-generated activities directly than activities obtained from Internet sources. Qualitative findings indicated that ChatGPT supported idea generation, access to instructional content, lesson-plan development, and time efficiency, while participants also reported limitations such as insufficient or repetitive content, misalignment with learning objectives, and system-related problems. Overall, ChatGPT may support lesson planning when its outputs are critically evaluated and adapted to pedagogical needs.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: Cheating or being cheated? Academic integrity and a changing cheating habitus in international AI governance discourse
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence in higher education is transforming how academic work is produced and legitimized, raising questions about the governance of academic integrity. Current discussions tend to frame integrity as student misconduct, giving less attention to shifts in institutional expectations and educational practices associated with AI-assisted learning. This study examines how international AI policy discourse constructs academic integrity in higher education and allocates responsibility for ethical AI use among institutional actors. Drawing on Bourdieu's theory of practice and Laclau's notion of floating signifiers, it proposes the changing cheating habitus as an analytical concept for examining how dispositions towards authorship and legitimate academic participation might change with the conditions of academic work. The study applies Critical Discourse Analysis to four UNESCO and OECD publications issued between 2023 and 2026, comprising institutional guidance, policy outlooks and a UNESCO-commissioned anthology. Fairclough's three-dimensional framework is used to examine how academic integrity is constructed across the textual, discursive and social dimensions of policy discourse. The findings suggest that responsibility, transparency, trust, authenticity and responsible use act as floating signifiers. They provide normative coherence but remain operationally underdefined across institutional contexts. This ambiguity is embedded in contemporary AI governance discourse. Its effects arise through the relationship between policy language, institutional interpretation and established academic conventions. Institutions promote AI integration through narratives of innovation while continuing to regulate academic legitimacy through assumptions of independent authorship and visible intellectual labour. This creates a structural mismatch in which students are encouraged to engage in AI-supported academic work while remaining accountable to integrity frameworks that have not evolved accordingly. The analysis also suggests that enforcement mechanisms may operate as academic capital filters if differences in academic capital affect the visibility of AI-assisted work. The study defines cheating and being cheated as concurrent structural outcomes arising from governance frameworks that encourage AI use while retaining accountability mechanisms developed before generative AI. It presents academic integrity as structurally mediated and negotiated through discourse. The analysis informs educational leadership and AI governance, especially in rapidly changing contexts such as the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf region.

items.title: Chinese private university EFL students’ attitude towards iWrite Automated Essay Scoring system: influencing mechanism from perceived interactivity to criticism
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been prominent in our daily lives by means of mobile applications and web search engines. AI-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES) system is playing an increasingly important role in higher education field. This study investigated the relationship between Chinese private university EFL students’ perceived interactivity of iWrite AES system and perceived performance, confirmation, individual innovativeness of AES system, as well as their reflective thinking, and how the variables influence students’ criticism of AES system. Based on a sample of 442 students, the study used Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) for data analysis. The findings indicated that students’ perceived interactivity of AES system is positively related to perceived performance and confirmation. Students’ perceived performance of AES system has a significant influence on students’ confirmation. Furthermore, students’ confirmation of AES system positively affects individual innovativeness, reflective thinking and criticism of AES. And students’ individual innovativeness also positively influences students’ reflective thinking of AES. However, students’ individual innovativeness and reflective thinking of AES system doesn’t have a positive relationship with students’ criticism. This study not only reveals Chinese private university EFL students’ attitudes and experiences towards technological tools but also provide valuable support for enhancing teaching effectiveness and improving teaching methods.

items.title: Clinical Phenotypes, Machine‐Learning Risk Stratification and Treatment Outcomes of Constipation in Stroke Patients Receiving Enteral Nutrition: A Retrospective Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. AIM: This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. STUDY DESIGN: Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. RESULTS: Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. CONCLUSIONS: Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.

items.title: Close the Gap or Widen It? AI, Equity and Learning at the Weakest Link
items.abstract: Generative AI could be the most powerful equaliser in the history of education, putting a patient, personalised tutor within reach of every child. It could equally widen the gap between advantaged and disadvant‐ aged learners, because new technologies usually reach those with re‐ sources first and those without last, if at all. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside data on connectivity, refugee education, aid and AI develop‐ ment policy. It argues that the outcome will not be decided by the techno‐ logy but by deliberate choices, and that leaving AI to markets and chance will produce the worse outcome. It identifies four layers of the AI divide: access, skilled guidance, language and culture, and recognition of what learners achieve. It then examines the weakest link in global education, learners in crisis and displacement, where 5.8 million refugee children were out of school in 2025 and international aid fell by nearly a quarter in a single year. It reviews approaches that work where power, connectivity and funding cannot be assumed, including offline platforms, AI delivered through basic phones, support for community teachers and portable, re‐ cognised certificates, along with their risks. It proposes a six-question equity test for any AI decision in education.

items.title: Co-Creating a Humane Trading Architecture: Enterprise, Innovation and the Bangladesh–European Union Economic Partnership — A Research Paper on Market Measurement, Digital Sovereignty and Phased Integration
items.abstract: Bangladesh's impending transition from least-developed-country status and the initialling of a Framework Agreement on Comprehensive Partnership and Cooperation with the European Union open a structured opportunity to redesign the bilateral economic relationship. This paper develops the concept of a humane trading architecture in which enterprise competitiveness and innovation capacity function as the principal transmission mechanisms between preferential market access and structural transformation. It integrates multidimensional market-measurement tools (the Economic Vulnerability Index and the Environmental Performance Index), mild-form transaction authentication and data validation for small and medium enterprise trade finance, sovereign computational capacity (including a Bangla large language model embedded in digital public infrastructure), and post-quantum readiness for trade finance. Drawing on comparative lessons from the EU–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement and EU–India negotiations, the paper specifies five negotiating redlines, co-creation pathways in food, fuel and finance, and a three-phase roadmap calibrated to the current United Nations graduation schedule and the pending request for a preparatory extension. The resulting framework preserves strategic autonomy while extending economic franchise to domestic firms and workers. Personal academic views only.

items.title: CoFrame: A System for Training Novice Cobot Programmers
items.abstract: The introduction of collaborative robots (cobots) into the workplace has presented both opportunities and challenges for those seeking to utilize their functionality. Prior research has shown that despite the capabilities afforded by cobots, there is a disconnect between those capabilities and the applications in which they are currently deployed, partially due to a lack of effective cobot-focused instruction in the field. Experts who work successfully within this collaborative domain could offer insight into the considerations and processes they use to more effectively capture this cobot capability. Using an analysis of expert insights in the collaborative interaction design space, we developed a set of Expert Frames based on these insights and integrated these Expert Frames into a new training and programming system and evaluated how automated expert feedback supports novice troubleshooting and user perception. We evaluated our system with novice and expert users to understand their experience and expectations for robot programming.

items.title: Cognitive abilities and trust calibration: Understanding individual differences in automation trust dynamics
items.abstract: Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people form and adjust trust in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities — working memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) — shape trust dynamics, particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures. Participants (N = 111) completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-65%-100%) while completing an arithmetic task. Results revealed that WM and Gf positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system reliability history. Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting that trust loss may occur rapidly after salient failures. The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about automation. These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration. This work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.

items.title: Cognitive engagement in blended learning of L2 writing: dimensions and influencing factors
items.abstract: This study explores the dimensions and influencing factors of Chinese students’ cognitive engagement in a blended learning environment that integrates offline classroom instruction with online written evaluation (including AI-driven automated written evaluation and human-based evaluation). By analyzing data from questionnaires, semi-structured interviews, writing drafts, and feedback, the findings reveal that: (1) students’ cognitive engagement in blended learning is indicated by their attention, cognitive and metacognitive operations, and self-regulation; (2) These dimensions are influenced by a combination of individual and contextual factors, including learner autonomy, study habits, motivation, exams, task difficulty, and instruction mode. This study has significant theoretical and practical implications for enhancing student engagement in blended learning and for the deeper integration of AI into second language (L2) writing instruction.

items.title: Compliance by Design: Governing AI ‐Augmented Quantitative Analysis in Clinical and Translational Research
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from promise to routine practice in clinical and translational research, and large language models (LLMs) are now used to scope analyses, draft and debug code, and accelerate the quantitative work that supports clinical and translational decisions. This adoption is outpacing the operational safeguards that keep such work reproducible and auditable, and the central risk is not only erroneous code but the quieter erosion of the analytical discipline on which trustworthy bench‐to‐bedside decisions depend. In this position paper, we argue that AI can be integrated into regulated quantitative workflows without sacrificing reproducibility, provided it operates inside a compliance‐by‐design architecture built on two principles: analytical intent must be formally encoded and locked before execution, and the analysis itself must run outside the LLM as specification‐verified code in a validated environment. We describe three failure modes that ordinary quality control does not detect, namely context drift, the displacement effect, and implementation drift, and we link each to documented model behavior. For open‐ended investigation, these principles are operationalized as a four‐step execution firewall; for recurring development studies such as assay validations and animal safety studies, they are operationalized through a governed library of documented, validated agents, supported by fit‐for‐purpose validation, a clear separation of human and machine roles, and post‐deployment monitoring. Both approaches can be implemented with components available today. Used this way, AI enhances rather than replaces quantitative expertise, which now resides less in the code a model produces than in the constraints a scientist defines before it runs.

items.title: Compliance with Occupational Health and Safety Requirements in Uganda's Construction Sector: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Construction is a high-risk industry and in Uganda it is regulated by the Occupational safety and Health Act, 2006. However, there is limited evidence on how well construction employers comply with their legal duties and why. This evidence gap has also not been reviewed. To identify, appraise and synthesize the evidence on compliance with occupational health and safety (OHS) requirements in Uganda's construction sector, the determinants of compliance and the regulatory and enforcement environment. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020. CORE (3 searches), Consensus and Google Scholar were searched and records imported into Zotero on 22 October 2026. A total of 226 records were identified, of which 157 unique records were screened. 8 reports out of 13 requested were assessed for eligibility. Studies were eligible if they investigated compliance, practices, injuries or regulation of OHS in Uganda's construction sector. We evaluated quality with a six-domain instrument. Results were thematically synthesized. Six studies from 2016 to 2023 were included: four cross-sectional or case studies, one regulatory review with key informant interviews and one master's thesis. Five themes emerged: the level of compliance and its measurement, organizational rather than personal determinants of compliance, outdated law and limited enforcement capacity, personal protective equipment as the most visible gap, differences between building and road sites and between firms. One study reported 95% compliance that its own scale classed as unacceptable and another reported an injury prevalence of 32.4%. No included study analyses inspection or prosecution data, or the construction-specific duties of employers under the 2006 Act. Compliance in Uganda's construction sector appears to be partial and organization-driven, with a regulatory framework described as outdated and weakly enforced. The evidence is limited, focused on Kampala and mainly cross-sectional. Five relevant reports could not be obtained. The priority areas include enforcement data, doctrinal analysis of employer duties and studies of small contractors and sites outside Kampala.

items.title: Conclusion
items.abstract: This conclusion draws together the book’s findings on the regulation of artificial intelligence deployed by social media platforms under African human rights law. It argues that the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights remains capable of robust purposive interpretation under digital conditions, and that its foundational norms of dignity, equality, and non-domination, together with its recognition of collective as well as individual rights, offer a distinctive basis for responding to algorithmic harm. The conclusion assesses the uneven progress made across the continent, acknowledging the operationalisation of regional data protection instruments and the growth of national legislation while identifying persistent fragmentation, limited enforcement capacity, and Africa’s position as a consumer rather than a co-creator of these technologies. It ends by setting out what a rights-based digital ecosystem would require.

items.title: Conscience in the Age of Algorithms: Ethical Dilemmas in Generative AI Use Across Faith-Based Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: This study explored the ethical tensions and dilemmas emerging across stakeholder groups- research administrators, faculty, and undergraduate students- regarding the use of Generative AI in academic research within faith-based higher education institutions in Mindanao, Philippines. A qualitative, holistic multiple-case study design was employed across five institutions, with fifteen participants (one administrator, one faculty member, and one student per institution) selected through purposive maximum variation sampling; semi-structured interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis for within-case analysis and Merriam’s five-step approach for cross-case synthesis. Nine essential themes emerged, three per stakeholder group, reflecting dilemmas of efficiency versus authentic learning, detection versus procedural fairness, innovation versus institutional integrity, assistance versus intellectual dependency, accuracy versus fabrication, professional judgment versus consistency, convenience versus genuine learning, confidence versus guilt and fear, and reliable detection versus equitable access to support, with institutional capacity emerging as a significant mediating factor that shaped both policy formalization and enforcement consistency. In addressing a contextual gap left by secular-focused studies, this research also fills a methodological gap: prior Philippine studies on faith-based AI governance relied largely on document analysis, whereas this study uses semi-structured interviews across three stakeholder groups within each institution, capturing lived experiences of ethical decision-making. The findings provide empirical evidence of how faith-based Philippine institutions navigate Gen AI ethical dilemmas and inform institutional policy design, faculty development, reform of detection practices, and student support mechanisms, particularly in resource-limited settings where ethical governance must be adapted to available capacity.

items.title: Conspiracy Theories Dominate Spanish Antivaccine Narratives on TikTok: A Content Analysis of Algorithmic and Linguistic Evasion
items.abstract: This study provides one of the first systematic examinations of Spanish-language antivaccine narratives on TikTok. Through a two-phase content analysis, we characterized antivaccine narratives on Spanish TikTok guided by the sociotechnical theory of media effects. A total of 186 vaccine posts were initially retrieved via hashtag searches conducted from Spain, with 100 antivaccine posts forming the final sample representing Spanish-language content from across Hispanic communities on TikTok. Findings indicate the dominance of conspiratorial narratives, propagated primarily by non-experts who frequently cite scientific sources to enhance credibility using TikTok features such as viral audio trends and coded lexical variations in Spanish (e.g., v4cun4, 3nf3rm3d4d, la pua, pinchazo) revealing how Spanish antivaccine narratives adapt to platform-specific features to evade detection. These narratives were linked to broader conspiracy theories, including Agenda 2030, 5 G, and the “global reset.” These results highlight persistent algorithmic blind spots for Spanish antivaccine content and underscore the need for language-specific detection and counter-messaging strategies.

items.title: Construct Validity of Frontier Large Language Models on 4 Spanish Health Professions Specialty-Access Examinations (MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR): Cross-Sectional Benchmarking and Psychometric Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on health-professions examinations. Whether these scores support the same interpretations as human scores remains uncertain. Spain uses parallel multiple-choice examinations for entry to specialty training in medicine (Médico Interno Residente [MIR]), nursing (Enfermero Interno Residente [EIR]), psychology (Psicólogo Interno Residente [PIR]), and pharmacy (Farmacéutico Interno Residente [FIR]). Objective Using the January 2026 MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR examinations, this study aimed to quantify the correspondence between human and LLM item facility and to describe model accuracy, distractor selection, and performance associated with measured surface features. Methods We evaluated 839 valid items using 12 configurations: GPT-5.2 at 3 reasoning efforts and Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic), each under neutral and expert prompts, with one run per configuration. The primary measure was the Spearman correlation (ρ) between human and machine facility on 828 complete paired items. We examined sensitivity to panel composition, scoring, pooling, and assumed reliability; compared distractor choices with a post hoc plausibility-weighted baseline; and evaluated a surface-feature classifier. Image analyses distinguished supplied from withheld images. An exploratory LLM-judge audit assessed generated explanations. Bootstrap CIs resample items or, for distractor concordance, error events; they exclude run-to-run uncertainty. Results The highest pooled accuracy was 94.8% (795/839); all 12 configurations answered 668 of 828 paired items correctly (80.7%). Scores clustered near the ceiling among the strongest configurations. Human and machine facility correlated at 0.40 (95% CI 0.34-0.45), with estimates of 0.31 to 0.40 across panel definitions and 0.39 (95% CI 0.33-0.45) after exam-stratified pooling. The observed correlation was lower than predicted by a specified one-axis simulation with a uniform model advantage (0.63; predictive interval 0.59 to 0.66; P <.001). Among 672 model errors, dominant human-distractor selection differed from the plausibility-weighted baseline by –1.25 percentage points (95% CI –4.53 to 2.19), compatible with no difference. Surface-feature accuracy was 34.4% (289/839), similar to selecting the longest option (34.6%, 290/839). The adjusted association with model correctness was uncertain (odds ratio [OR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.72-1.04). Image-associated accuracy was lower both when images were supplied (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.21-0.53) and when withheld (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.08-0.16). Conclusions In this single 2026 cohort, high LLM scores coexisted with limited separation among the strongest configurations and moderate correspondence with human item difficulty. These findings caution against interpreting model scores as equivalent evidence of human competence. They do not establish clinical performance or invalidate the examinations for human candidates.

items.title: Construction and Empirical Research on Classroom Teaching Evaluation Model of Vocational Education Based on Artificial Intelligence Multimodal Data Fusion
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of policies promoting quality enhancement and excellence in vocational education alongside educational evaluation reforms, traditional classroom teaching assessments struggle to comprehensively reflect teaching quality due to limitations such as single-dimensional data and insufficient technological empowerment. To address this, this study constructs an AI-driven multimodal data fusion model for classroom teaching evaluation. This model encompasses a five-layer technical architecture—data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, metric calculation, and result feedback—integrating three types of multi-source heterogeneous information: teaching behavior data (based on DBSCAN clustering analysis), physiological state data (combined with ResNet-18 emotion recognition), and dynamic effect data (using TransE knowledge transfer evaluation). This enables comprehensive and precise diagnosis of the classroom teaching process. Empirical validation was conducted in smart classroom environments using S-T behavioral analysis, engagement curves, and the Rt-Ch model. Results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in identifying critical issues such as imbalanced teaching pacing and fluctuating student engagement, significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness and objectivity of evaluations. This research not only provides a replicable technical pathway for diagnosing vocational education classroom quality but also offers theoretical support and practical examples for the deep integration of artificial intelligence and educational assessment.

items.title: Consumers or Producers? The Feedback–Autonomy Paradox of AI Tools in Blended ESP Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now reach English for Specific Purposes (ESP) students through the smartphones they already carry, often before institutions have decided how these tools should be used. This qualitative case study examines how ESP students and teachers at a university in the Sultanate of Oman experienced AI-supported feedback in blended learning, and how the appeal of immediate feedback interacted with the need for learner autonomy. The data come from a wider doctoral study of mobile technology in ESP classes and comprise semi-structured interviews with ESP teachers, five focus groups with 30 second-year students from maritime, engineering and medical programmes, 81 open-ended questionnaire responses and three classroom observations. AI use was not a preset topic; it emerged from participants’ own accounts of the applications they used. Students described ChatGPT and AI speaking applications as an always-available, non-judgmental tutor that gave immediate feedback and helped them rehearse speaking, writing and professional communication with more confidence. Teachers welcomed this but worried that students might become consumers rather than producers of language. We interpret these accounts as a feedback–autonomy paradox: the support that builds confidence can also crowd out independent effort, while autonomy without guidance leaves learners unsure of their progress. Teachers managed the paradox through dialogical use of AI, recorded practice followed by peer or teacher feedback, and professionally authentic tasks, while cost, limited training and the absence of shared guidance constrained equitable access. We argue that the feedback–autonomy balance should be treated as a design decision that changes over the course of a programme, and we outline implications for ESP teachers and institutions.

items.title: Conventionally Developed Versus Large Language Model-Generated Exam Tasks in Higher Education: A Comparative Analysis
items.abstract: This exploratory field study investigates how human-screened exam tasks generated by the large language model (LLM) GPT-4o perform in comparison with conventionally developed exam tasks with regard to selected quality criteria. Using two business administration modules at a German distance-learning university, human-screened LLM-generated tasks were integrated into submission assignments (SA) alongside instructor-created tasks. Four selected task-quality indicators were examined: objective difficulty, subjective difficulty, context relevance, and item discrimination. The analysis combines descriptive statistics with paired-sample t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, applied at three aggregation levels: SA-specific, module-level, and cross-module. The results revealed mixed and task-specific patterns. While selected indicators were numerically similar for some task pairs, statistically significant and, in one comparison, substantial differences were observed in others, particularly in objective difficulty. Given that the study examined only four task pairs that were not systematically matched and that prior human screening was conducted, the findings establish neither equivalence nor general comparability. However, the study provides initial exploratory insights from two business administration modules that can serve as a foundation for further research.

items.abstract: Background Scientific argumentation ability is an integrated ability in AI era. However, it’s difficult to improve learners’ scientific argumentation ability in traditional classes due to individual differences.Purpose Therefore, this study decomposed scientific argumentation ability based on the CER+R (Claim–Evidence–Reasoning–Rebuttal) fra mework and integrated these components to construct a scientific argumentation AI agent. This approach goes beyond traditional methods and makes the cultivation of scientific argumentation ability a data-driven and personalized process.Sample Participants were 18 university students enrolled in an Ecology course at a university in eastern China, with similar educational backgrounds and comparable initial performance.Design and methods A crossover experimental design was adopted, with two groups experiencing opposite sequences of AI-agent access: one used the agent first and then practiced independently, while the other practiced independently before using the agent. Guided by the ICAP and CER+R frameworks, epistemic network analysis (ENA) and lag sequential analysis (LSA) were used to examine learners’ cognition and argumentation behaviors, respectively. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were conducted to assess scientific argumentation performance.Results Students who practiced independently before gaining access to the AI agent demonstrated more interactive and constructive engagement. Their argumentation behaviors generally followed the CER+R framework, although rebuttals often lacked subsequent evidence or reasoning. Among the 12 students with complete test data, scientific argumentation performance improved significantly from pre-test to mid-test and post-test. Questionnaire results also showed increases in students’ trust in AI and engagement.Conclusion The findings suggest that a CER+R-based AI agent may support the development of scientific argumentation performance and positive learning attitudes. Introducing AI support after independent exploration may encourage deeper engagement, while additional scaffolding is needed to help students integrate rebuttals into complete arguments.

items.title: Craniopharyngioma.AI: An Explainable Ensemble Learning Framework for Personalized Craniopharyngioma Outcome Prediction
items.abstract: Introduction Craniopharyngiomas are rare sellar/suprasellar tumors with long-term postoperative morbidity, including permanent diabetes insipidus (DI) and tumor recurrence. Existing clinical tools offer limited individualized prognostication. We introduce a pilot artificial intelligence (AI) platform to hypothesize postoperative outcomes in craniopharyngioma surgery. Methods Patients with histologically confirmed craniopharyngioma who underwent surgical resection between 2008 and 2023 at a single institution were retrospectively analyzed. Clinical, radiographic, and intraoperative features (e.g., tumor dimensions, volume, intraventricular extension, surgical approach, and extent of resection) were modeled using machine learning algorithms with a unified ensemble pipeline to predict permanent DI and tumor recurrence. Explainable AI interpretation using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) quantified individual feature-level contributions, which were integrated into a FastAPI-powered web application for interactive prediction. Results 59 patients were used in a stratified cross-validation model training, of whom permanent DI occurred in 65.5% and tumor recurrence was recorded in 28.8%. The blended Ridge-Catboost ensemble achieved the highest performance for permanent DI prediction (AUC: 0.77±0.05, F1: 0.81±0.04), and a blended Naïve Bayes-Catboost ensemble was chosen for recurrence prediction (AUC: 0.78±0.12, F1: 0.67±0.15). SHAP-based feature ranking revealed that pre-operative BMI, age, and endocrine or visual dysfunction were the strongest predictors of DI and recurrence. Surgical approach and postoperative BMI changes further modulated DI risk. The app can be accessed at tinyurl.com/craniopharyngiomas. Conclusion In this small, single-institution cohort, ensemble learning and model tuning helped stabilize model accuracy and discriminative power. This exploratory AI prototype for prognostication might eventually support data-driven risk assessment in skull base oncology.

items.title: Critical AI literacy as a buffer against AI overtrust in students
items.abstract: Abstract Background The growing use of AI tools such as ChatGPT in academic settings has raised concerns about AI overtrust, yet its psychological correlates remain poorly understood. This study examined how academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation are associated with AI overtrust, and tested the sequential mediating roles of performance expectancy and AI literacy in these relationships. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 university students in South Korea who had prior experience using AI tools for academic purposes. The questionnaire measured academic self-efficacy, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, AI literacy, and AI overtrust. Serial mediation analysis was conducted using the PROCESS macro [1] to test direct and indirect effects, including pathways sequentially mediated by performance expectancy and AI literacy. Indirect effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap samples with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals. Results Academic self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation were both positively associated with AI overtrust: learners who reported higher confidence and greater autonomy also reported higher overtrust in AI-generated information. Extrinsic motivation was numerically more strongly associated with AI overtrust than intrinsic motivation. AI literacy was not significantly correlated with AI overtrust at the bivariate level, but showed a significant negative indirect association within the mediation model. Sequential mediation analysis further indicated that, across all three psychological traits, higher performance expectancy combined with higher AI literacy was associated with lower AI overtrust. Conclusions These findings suggest that learners with higher academic self-efficacy and stronger intrinsic motivation also tend to report higher AI overtrust. Although greater academic self-efficacy may reflect more autonomous use of AI tools, it was nonetheless associated with higher overtrust in the present sample. AI literacy education tailored to learners’ psychological profiles may help support critical thinking, ethical awareness, and responsible AI use.

items.title: Cross-Modal Learning and Retrieval Embeddings
items.abstract: With the multimedia information growing fast and fierce, intelligent systems have to be able to understand and relate information in different data modalities in a seamless manner. The current chapter is an overview of cross-modal learning and retrieval embeddings, the techniques of which are aimed at aligning text, images, audio, and video into common semantic spaces. It presents the general ideas of multimodal representation learning, such as modality-specific feature extraction, common latent space modeling and fusion strategies. The chapter discusses embedding strategies of both canonical correlation analysis and deep contrastive techniques and transformer-based multimodal networks. Important similarity measures and metric learning methods that facilitate a successful retrieval are discussed. A discussion on practical cross-modal retrieval systems, evaluation benchmarks, scalability issues, and deployment issues aims at bringing the theory into contact with the real world implementation. As well, robustness, bias and ethical responsibility are discussed. New research directions include foundation model unification and fine-grained alignment, which are used in shaping scalable and reliable multimedia intelligence systems.

items.title: Cultivating an ethos of attribution as an assessment practice in a postplagiarism era
items.abstract: This chapter explores the evolving landscape of academic integrity in the age of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), proposing a shift from rule-based referencing towards a more relational ethos of attribution. Drawing on the postplagiarism framework, Eaton distinguishes between referencing as a technical, commodified practice and attribution as a relational, reflective act of acknowledging intellectual lineage. Eaton critiques the economic motivations behind style guide publishers and the punitive nature of citation compliance in assessment, arguing that such practices often prioritise form over substance. In contrast, attribution fosters metacognitive awareness, evaluative judgement, and communal learning. The discussion extends to the complexities introduced by GenAI, highlighting the need for ethical co-creation and responsible authorship. The chapter concludes with a call for a recalibration of assessment practices and the development of an open-access, universal citation system that supports both academic rigour and ethical engagement with knowledge.

items.title: Curriculum Development for AI Literacy in Schools
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has infiltrated the digital landscape of children at an extremely fast rate, affecting the way children learn, communicate and access information. This chapter in the book makes a case in favor of an all-encompassing curriculum in AI literacy that will help children understand how to critically analyze the systems of algorithms, defend against subtle persuasion, and identify fake media. Based on the Critical Media Literacy Theory, Persuasion Knowledge Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Digital Resilience Frameworks, describes a modular, age-based curriculum between primary-level and secondary education. Experiential learning, gamification, and project-based assessments are some of the pedagogical strategies favored with the help of teacher training and alignment of policies. Finally, the chapter makes AI literacy a key factor to creating digitally resilient citizens who are capable of operating in algorithmically mediated spaces in a responsible, reflective and ethical manner.

items.title: Curriculum Development for Schools to Teach Children How to Recognize and Critically Evaluate AI Content
items.abstract: Children today are growing up in digital environments where Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a central yet often invisible role in shaping their experiences. From personalized recommendations and AI-generated academic assistance to targeted advertising and algorithmically curated content intelligent systems influence how children access information, form preferences, and make decisions. This chapter argues that AI literacy must be recognized as an essential component of contemporary school education. Drawing on an interdisciplinary review of literature in AI literacy, media studies, and education, the chapter proposes a curriculum-oriented framework based on three interconnected dimensions: operational, sociocultural and critical literacy. In response, it introduces a practical pedagogical approach centered on “questioning the machine,” encouraging students to develop habits of inquiry, reflection and ethical awareness in their interactions with AI-driven content.

items.title: CXRG-SVLM: a parameter-efficient small vision-language model for multi-view chest X-ray report generation in resource-constrained environments
items.abstract: Abstract Automated chest X-ray report generation reduces reporting delays in resource-constrained clinical environments. Existing vision-language models often rely on large language models or full fine-tuning. This dependence causes high computational costs and limits on-premise deployment. We propose CXRG-SVLM. This small vision-language model combines a frozen RAD-DINO medical image encoder with a 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-3B language model adapted using 4-bit QLoRA. A multi-view fusion module integrates frontal and lateral radiographs into a compact continuous visual representation. The resulting visual tokens are projected into the language-model embedding space and concatenated with clinical-indication embeddings to form a conditioning prefix. The decoder uses its native causal self-attention over this prefix and the generated tokens to produce the Findings report. The assembled implementation reports approximately 1.99 billion loaded parameter elements, of which approximately 38.1 million are trainable, corresponding to 1.91% of this framework-reported inventory. We evaluated the model on the Indiana University Chest X-ray dataset to generate the Findings section of the radiology report. The proposed model attains a ROUGE-L score of 0.3527 and a METEOR score of 0.2744. Automated entity-level agreement varies across findings, with the strongest F1 for normal descriptors and measurable agreement for pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and mediastinal mentions under the reported rule-based evaluation. Efficiency testing shows an average generation time of 5.27 seconds per report on a single graphics processing unit. These results establish the model’s computational feasibility and motivate subsequent radiologist evaluation of factual correctness, safety, and practical usefulness. Ultimately, CXRG-SVLM demonstrates that a parameter-efficient approach with less than 2% trainable parameters maintains competitive semantic fidelity, establishing an accessible foundation for future, prospectively validated on-premise clinical decision-support tools.

items.title: Data-driven assessment competencies for AIoT-enhanced traffic management: A framework for educators
items.abstract: This paper, developed through a literature-informed conceptual synthesis, focused on how integrating Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things (AIoT) enables new approaches to urban traffic management through intelligent data collection, real-time analytics, and automated decision-making. Despite rapid technological advances, existing curricula and assessment frameworks provide little guidance for competency-based assessment, learning analytics, and institutional implementation in AIoT-enhanced traffic management education. Accordingly, the authors developed conceptual frameworks that support competency-based assessment and institutional implementation for AIoT-enhanced traffic management education. Drawing on contemporary literature in AIoT, competency-based education, learning analytics, authentic assessment, and digital education, two complementary conceptual frameworks were develop. The proposed Data-Driven Assessment Competency Framework (DACF) is associated competency domains, learning outcomes, authentic assessment tasks, evidence sources, AI-assisted analytics, educator judgement, analytic rubrics, feedback, and competency decisions. The accompanying AIoT Assessment Implementation Framework (AAIF) provides direction for strategic alignment, curriculum integration, infrastructure development, educator capacity building, and continuous evaluation to support sustainable institutional implementation. The authors further present competency progression levels, worked examples of assessments, analytic rubrics, assessment weighting, human-in-the-loop assessment practices, and quality assurance processes to support transparent and evidence-informed competency assessment. Unlike existing competency, digital education, or AI literacy frameworks, DACF and AAIF integrate competency mapping, authentic assessment, learning analytics, multi-source evidence, educator judgement, and institutional implementation within a unified model tailored to AIoT-enhanced traffic management education. Finally, the paper presents policy recommendations, a structured validation roadmap, and future research priorities to guide empirical validation and advance AIoT-enhanced traffic management education for smart city mobility.

items.abstract: This chapter examines structured decision-making in investigative contexts, emphasising the Senior Investigating Officer’s responsibility to apply transparent, evidence-led processes, avoid cognitive pitfalls, and maintain defensible and auditable rationales under scrutiny. It contrasts fast-time and slow-time decision-making, analyses intuition, heuristics, bias, and situational awareness, and promotes deliberate analytical approaches to reduce error and improve operational effectiveness. The chapter advances an investigative mindset grounded in openness, scepticism, and structured reasoning, supported by the ABC rule, critical thinking, and systematic problem-solving models that prioritise multiple hypotheses and continuous review. It explains risk management principles, including threat, harm, and risk assessment, alongside structured frameworks such as the National Decision Model and the 5WH model to guide information-gathering and decision-making. Finally, the chapter reinforces learning through hypothesis-testing, reflective practice, and continuous review, strengthening professional judgement and supporting ethical, adaptive decision-making in complex investigations.

items.title: Defining Industry 4.0 and the Fourth Industrial Revolution
items.abstract: Industry 4.0 is frequently described through its technologies: cyber-physical systems, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, advanced analytics, cloud and edge computing, robotics, digital twins and platform infrastructures. Such descriptions are useful, but incomplete. They explain what has become technically possible but do not adequately explain why the organisational and human consequences are so substantial. This chapter therefore defines Industry 4.0 and the wider Fourth Industrial Revolution through a socio-technical systems perspective. It distinguishes the industrial concept of Industry 4.0 from the broader societal idea of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, examines the convergence and interdependence that differentiate the present transition from earlier waves of digitisation, and considers the implications for work, knowledge, authority, identity and institutional arrangements. The central argument is that Industry 4.0 is best understood as a reconfiguration of relationships among people, technologies, organisations and institutions. Its significance lies not in the presence of intelligent technologies alone, but in the redistribution of sensing, interpretation and decision-making across human and machine actors. Human transformation is consequently not an adjunct to technological adoption. It is a constitutive element of the transformation itself.

items.title: Deriving Metacognitive Scaffolding Design Principles and an Integrated Model for Generative AI–Supported Major Exploration
items.abstract: As flexible major selection systems, including undeclared admission, become increasingly widespread in higher education, learners' capacity for self-directed academic and career planning has become more important than ever.Although the widespread adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) has improved the efficiency of information acquisition, it also raises concerns about intensified cognitive offloading, whereby learners become overly dependent on AI-generated responses without engaging in critical thinking.To address this issue, this study proposes an AI-based integrated metacognitive scaffolding model that enables learners to use AI not merely as an information provider, but as a tool for expanding their thinking.To this end, an integrative literature review explored the theoretical relationship between metacognition and scaffolding, and a cross-mapping analysis was used to derive stage-specific design principles.In addition, a scenario-based walkthrough examined the logical applicability of the proposed model.The analysis suggests that AI-supported major exploration can be conceptually organized around the role of an Inquiring Coach.The proposed model organizes the learning process into three metacognitive phases-Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation-and specifies stage-specific strategies, including delaying immediate answers, detecting inconsistencies and generating counter-questions, and promoting reflective self-explanation.The model also incorporates a Fading mechanism as a design principle intended to support the gradual development of learners' selfdirected exploration.This study provides conceptual design guidelines for AI-supported career education systems.It proposes a theoretical basis for shifting attention from information-delivery efficiency to designing interactions that support learners' thinking.However, the model's effects on learners' metacognition or career decision-making were not empirically tested.

items.title: Design and analysis of an affordable manual sit-to-stand wheelchair for disabled individuals
items.abstract: Purpose The individuals with lower-limb disabilities often experience considerable difficulty during sit-to-stand (STS) transitions, limiting their independence and increasing reliance on caregivers. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO, 2023), nearly 80 million people worldwide require wheelchairs.Method This study presents the design and performance evaluation of an affordable manual sit-to-stand wheelchair that incorporates ergonomic and anthropometric design principles with a three-bar linkage mechanism, ball screw drive, scissor-lift structure, force-balancing mechanism, and optimised gear ratio to ensure stable, controlled, and energy-efficient operation without electrical actuators. Structural validation of design using finite element analysis demonstrated a maximum frame deformation of 2.2 mm and a factor of safety of 2.5 under a static load of 120 kg, confirming the mechanical reliability of the design. Human testing is conducted with 25 participants (15 wheelchair users and 10 healthy volunteers), while clinical evaluation is performed under a physiotherapist’s supervision using standardised functional assessment protocols.Result The average sit-to-stand transition time is 9.5 ± 1.8 s, with 90% of participants achieving successful independent standing. Force analysis indicated that the proposed linkage mechanism reduced the operating force to approximately 10 N, corresponding to a 45.6% reduction in user effort. Furthermore, usability assessment yielded a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 86.3/100, indicating excellent user acceptance.Conclusion The findings demonstrate that the proposed STS wheelchair is a safe, mechanically robust, and cost-effective assistive mobility solution that enhances user independence, reduces caregiver burden, and improves the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments, particularly in low-resource settings.

items.title: Design and Field Validation of a VR-Based RAG Historical NPC: Knowledge Grounding and Persona Grounding Can Fail Independently
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based non-player characters (NPCs) can support unscripted historical dialogue, but their behavior in deployed educational virtual reality (VR) settings remains underexamined. This study reports the design and field validation of a self-hosted VR platform in which a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) NPC, representing King Sejong the Great, engaged 42 international participants across 126 intercultural-learning sessions. The analytic corpus, reconstructed from retained session logs, comprised 104 sessions from 39 participants (2053 participant turns; 2053 NPC responses). Repetitive NPC response loops occurred in 33 sessions (31.7%), spanning 54 episodes and 190 responses, and co-occurred with learner-side transcript repetition in 31 of these sessions. The NPC maintained its first-person persona throughout the screened corpus, yet produced 30 biographical claims unsupported by the historical record: persona consistency did not ensure factual grounding. Prompt compliance varied by instruction type, and a post hoc implementation audit could not confirm that retrieved content contributed to individual responses. Together, these results identify persona grounding, knowledge grounding, retrieval observability, and session-level instrumentation as validation targets that deployed VR–LLM systems must address separately.

items.title: DESIGN METHODS FOR RESPONSIVE COMMERCIAL WEBSITE INTERFACES BASED ON MOBILE INTERACTION PATTERNS
items.abstract: In the current digital landscape, the success of mobile commerce is tied directly to the quality of the user interface. This study examines how shifting to a "Mobile First" philosophy fundamentally reshapes the architecture of web applications. We look beyond mere technical specifications to explore the physics of user-screen interaction—from the ergonomics of "active finger" movements to reducing page weight by stripping away bulky third-party frameworks. Our research demonstrates that leveraging native HTML5/CSS3 code alongside flexible layouts (Grid and Flexbox) creates interfaces that are not only lightning-fast but also intuitively adaptive to human behavior.

items.title: Designing assessment for GenAI contexts
items.abstract: This chapter argues that defensive responses to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and academic integrity, while understandable, focus on the wrong problem. Rather than asking how to contain or neutralise GenAI, we might ask how its emergence exposes long-standing weaknesses in assessment design and opens opportunities for transformation. Learning has always been collective and distributed across people, technologies, and contexts, yet dominant systems continue to treat knowledge as the property of isolated learners. Drawing on an entangled pedagogy perspective, the chapter challenges the individualistic assumptions underpinning traditional assessment. GenAI makes the fiction of autonomous academic work visible, exposing the fragility of product-based, grade-focused assessment. Reconceptualising academic integrity as collective, relational, and situated rather than individual and rule-based, this chapter argues for framing it not by what students must avoid but by what they must learn to do: engage ethically and purposefully with resources, including AI, while navigating complex learning contexts. Assessment is reimagined as codesigned and collaborative, with students actively shaping criteria, parameters, and outcomes. In this vision, assessment cultivates the adaptive capacity required for professional and social life, where competence emerges through collectively orchestrating human and technological resources in ways that reflect the entangled nature of learning in a complex world.

items.title: Designing Backup-Supporting Information Displays for Multi-Human Multi-Agent Teams in Drone Swarm Supervision
items.abstract: Search-and-rescue (SAR) drone swarms increasingly require multi-operator supervision, in which backup behaviors redistribute cognitive load to improve performance but introduce trade-offs in situational awareness (SA) and task engagement. Existing human-autonomy teaming interfaces present symmetric displays across all roles, ignoring the asymmetric information needs of backup providers and recipients. We developed a two-human, eight-drone Unity SAR testbed that operationalizes three team structures (independent, Operator A-busy, Operator B-busy) via event-allocation manipulation, with a SPAM (Situation Present Assessment Method)-derived in-task SA probe. Three iterative focus groups with eight human-centered design researchers and professionals yielded four display conditions: no-display baseline, effort display, urgency display, and combined. Semi-structured interviews with three SAR practitioners confirmed high realism ratings for the overall testbed and the viability of dynamic backup. A feasibility pilot study ( N = 4) revealed a significant main effect of team structure on backup count, confirming that the manipulation elicits backup behaviors as designed.

items.title: Designing for Social Presence in AR/MR: Dimensions, Patterns, and Research Directions
items.abstract: The rise of virtual reality (VR), mixed reality (MR), and augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays (HMDs) has expanded the design space for social extended reality (XR) systems. However, creating realistic social XR experiences with high social presence remains challenging. Based on a screening of 3,414 studies and thematic analysis of 250 papers published between 2015 and 2021, followed by a validation of the resulting design space through the categorization of 258 studies published between 2022 and 2026, we identify (1) seven common social interaction patterns in AR/MR, (2) thirteen design dimensions for supporting all levels of social presence while developing social AR/MR solutions, (3) future research opportunities, and (4) a practitioner guide that translates the extracted design dimensions into actionable design considerations. Through our work, researchers, developers, and designers can develop realistic, engaging social AR/MR solutions that foster social connection and bring minds closer together.
